title: Nursing
tagline: The dedicated RN path — prerequisites, NCLEX, first job, specialties, and advanced practice.
summary: A deep-dive specialization of the Healthcare Careers roadmap: nursing from prerequisites and nursing school through NCLEX licensure, the med-surg first job, specialty certification, and the branch points into advanced practice, leadership, education, and travel nursing.

detail.description: Nursing tiers: CNA (assistive), LPN/LVN (basic licensed care), RN (the professional core), and APRNs (nurse practitioners, CRNAs, midwives, educators) — each with its own license and scope.
detail.why: Mapping the ladder first lets you plan the cheapest, fastest route to the tier you actually want — many people over- or under-shoot.
learn: Compare scope and education for CNA, LPN, RN, APRN
Read the BLS OOH registered-nurse profile
Interview or shadow one nurse per tier if possible
Pick a 5-year target tier and work backward

detail.description: Nursing programs screen hard on prerequisites — anatomy & physiology I/II, microbiology, chemistry, statistics, and developmental psychology — with competitive GPA cutoffs.
detail.why: Prereq GPA is the single biggest admissions lever; taking them deliberately (one science per term, with support) protects your options.
learn: List your target programs' exact prereq courses and minimum grades
Schedule sciences one per term with lab sections
Use tutoring and office hours from day one
Track your science GPA separately

detail.description: Working as a CNA during prereqs builds patient-contact fundamentals — vitals, mobility, hygiene, and being inside a facility — and strengthens nursing-school applications substantially.
detail.why: Programs admit CNAs at higher rates, and the floor experience tells you early whether the work's physical and emotional reality fits.
learn: Complete a state CNA program (weeks-long) and get listed
Work part-time or per-diem during prereqs
Practice vitals, charting, and priority awareness
Collect a reference from your nurse supervisor

resources.title: BLS OOH — Nursing Assistants and Orderlies

detail.description: Three RN entry routes: ADN (2-year, cheapest, fastest to license), BSN (4-year, preferred by Magnet hospitals and required by many), and direct-entry/accelerated programs for degree-holders.
detail.why: The route choice is a cost-speed-vs-options trade — and bridge programs (ADN→BSN) make starting cheaper without closing doors.
learn: Compare total cost and timelines of each route locally
Check BSN preferences at hospitals you'd target
Verify NCLEX pass rates for programs you consider
Note accelerated BSN options if you hold any bachelor's

detail.description: Admissions combine the TEAS (Test of Essential Academic Skills) or similar entrance exams with GPA, essays, and references — spaces are limited and ranked.
detail.why: Applying widely and early, with a prepared TEAS score, is the difference between waiting a semester and starting on time.
learn: Take a full TEAS practice test for a baseline
Study weak domains (often math and science) for 6–8 weeks
Apply to 3–5 programs including community colleges
Write essays from real clinical-adjacent experiences

detail.description: Nursing school layers pharmacology, med-surg, fundamentals, and specialty rotations on escalating clinical hours — with NCLEX-style testing from semester one.
detail.why: Surviving school is a systems problem: study groups, question banks, and protecting sleep beat last-minute cramming.
learn: Build a weekly study system around question banks
Master pharmacology cards (the classic filter course)
Form a clinical-prep routine the night before rotations
Use faculty office hours early, not after failing grades

detail.description: Rotations through med-surg, pediatrics, OB, psych, and community settings turn classroom knowledge into patient care under supervision — and quietly audition you for jobs.
detail.why: Units hire nurses they've met on clinicals; treat every rotation day as a working interview.
learn: Prepare care plans the night before every clinical
Ask nurses on each unit what they wish they'd known
Note which populations energize you per rotation
Request references from clinical instructors you impress

detail.description: The NCLEX-RN (NCSBN) is the national licensure exam — adaptive testing across safe care, health promotion, psychosocial, and physiological integrity categories.
detail.why: It is the single gate to practice; a structured 6–8 week question-bank campaign after graduation is the proven approach.
learn: Study the NCSBN test plan by category weights
Build a 75–100 questions-per-day habit near the exam
Review every wrong answer's rationale immediately
Schedule within months of graduation while fresh

certs.name: RN License
certs.issuer: State boards of nursing (NCLEX-RN via NCSBN)
certs.note: Graduate from an approved program and pass the NCLEX-RN; licensure is by state with compact options.

detail.description: The LPN-first route licenses faster (~12 months), earns immediately, and bridges to RN through LPN-to-RN programs — trading some mobility for early income and experience.
detail.why: For career changers and budget-constrained students, LPN-first is a viable, dignified route with a clear RN bridge.
learn: Compare LPN wages/scope vs your RN timeline math
Find LPN-to-RN bridge programs in your state
Confirm bridge credit for LPN experience
Talk to an LPN who bridged about the reality

detail.description: Funding options stack: community-college ADN routes, employer tuition partnerships, hospital scholarship-for-service programs, federal aid, and loan-forgiveness programs tied to service.
detail.why: Nursing has unusually strong employer-funded pathways — graduating debt-light changes every later decision.
learn: Ask local hospitals about sponsorships and work commitments
Research federal loan-forgiveness for public/clinical service
Compare community-college vs university ADN/BSN costs
Apply for nursing-specific scholarships each year

detail.description: First jobs: residency programs (structured new-grad onboarding) vs direct med-surg hire; applications go out during final semester with references from clinicals.
detail.why: A real residency (with preceptors and classes) dramatically improves first-year survival — choose the program, not just the unit.
learn: Apply to new-grad residencies before graduation
Compare residency structures: length, preceptorship, classes
Polish a clinical-focused resume with your rotations
Practice the 'tell me about a patient' stories

detail.description: Medical-surgical nursing is the classic foundation: 4–7 patients, prioritization, time management, and the full breadth of adult conditions — where assessment instincts are forged.
detail.why: Even nurses destined for ICU or specialties benefit from a med-surg year; it teaches the prioritization muscle every unit assumes.
learn: Master shift organization: assessments, meds, charting cycles
Learn delegation to CNAs/LPNs within scope
Study one patient condition deeply per week
Ask for graduated patient loads as you improve
tasks: Assess patient health problems and needs, develop and implement nursing care plans, and maintain medical records.

detail.description: The nurse's core skill: systematic head-to-toe assessment, recognizing the deteriorating patient early, and escalating with SBAR communication that gets heard.
detail.why: Assessment instinct — noticing 'something is wrong' before numbers crash — is what separates safe nurses from great ones.
learn: Practice head-to-toe assessments to a 10-minute standard
Learn early-warning signs (respiratory, neuro, sepsis patterns)
Use SBAR for every escalation call
Debrief near-misses with preceptors

detail.description: Clinical documentation in Epic/Cerner-class EHRs: timely, objective, legally defensible charting, medication administration records, and care-plan updates.
detail.why: Charting is both a legal shield and the communication backbone of continuity — and it consumes real shift time to master.
learn: Learn SOAP-style and flowsheet documentation standards
Chart in real time, never batch at shift end
Practice objective language (what you saw/heard/did)
Understand late-entry and amendment rules

detail.description: Specialty choice — ICU, ED, OR, L&D, oncology, psych, pediatrics — shapes acuity, schedules, certifications, and long-term trajectory; most units want 1–2 years of foundation first.
detail.why: Choosing deliberately (by pace, patient population, and intensity) prevents the common two-year drift and burnout cycle.
learn: Shadow shifts on 2–3 units before transferring
Compare acuity, ratios, and schedules honestly
Identify which specialty certifications your targets require
Decide: depth (ICU/OR) vs breadth (ED, med-surg)

detail.description: Board certifications after practice hours — CCRN (critical care, AACN), OCN (oncology), CEN (emergency, ENA), RNC-OB (obstetrics) — mark expertise and often carry differential pay.
detail.why: Certifications are the profession's visible expertise layer; they open charge, educator, and transfer doors.
learn: Identify your specialty's certifying body and hour requirements
Plan certification after the required practice window
Use review courses aligned to the exam blueprint
Check your employer's certification pay and reimbursement

certs.name: CCRN
certs.note: Critical-care RN certification after required practice hours; exemplar of specialty nursing board certifications.

detail.description: First leadership roles: charge nurse (shift coordination, bed flow, staffing) and preceptor (teaching new nurses) — informal leadership that precedes formal management.
detail.why: Charge and preceptor work is how leadership aptitude becomes visible — and it's how units choose who they want to keep.
learn: Volunteer to precept nursing students and new grads
Learn bed-flow and staffing-phone rhythms as charge
Practice feedback conversations with juniors kindly
Document your teaching contributions for promotion files

detail.description: Advancement degrees: RN-to-BSN bridge (often online, employer-supported), then MSN tracks — education, leadership, informatics, or the APRN routes (NP, CRNA, CNM, CNS).
detail.why: Degrees unlock the ceiling: leadership tracks, educator roles, and every advanced-practice license sits on the MSN.
learn: Check employer tuition assistance for BSN/MSN
Compare MSN tracks against your 10-year goal
Verify accreditation and APRN pathways for NP/CRNA
Consider part-time study while working per-diem

detail.description: Advanced practice registered nurses: nurse practitioners (family, acute, psych, peds), CRNAs (anesthesia), nurse-midwives, and clinical nurse specialists — graduate education plus national certification and state licensure.
detail.why: APRN roles are the profession's most autonomous and best-compensated — with direct-patient-impact careers in every setting.
learn: Compare NP population foci and program formats
Note typical RN experience expectations per track
Research state practice-authority rules
Plan grad-program applications around experience hours

detail.description: Travel and per-diem nursing: contract assignments (typically 13 weeks) with housing stipends, premium pay, and location freedom — best after 1–2 years of solid acute-care foundation.
detail.why: Flex work lets nurses reset burnout, see the country, and test different health systems — with honest trade-offs in support and continuity.
learn: Build 1–2 years of in-demand acute experience first
Learn how agencies, stipends, and taxes actually work
Compare travel vs staff total compensation carefully
Start with one close-to-home contract as a trial

detail.description: Off-the-bedside branches: nurse manager and director tracks, clinical nurse educators, professional-development specialists, informatics, and quality/safety roles.
detail.why: Nursing's leadership ceiling is real and close — many CNOs started at the bedside, and education roles protect longevity.
learn: Shadow a nurse manager for a day
Explore clinical-nurse-educator roles at your hospital
Consider informatics if you love systems and data
Note the MSN/MHA expectations per leadership track

resources.title: BLS OOH — Medical and Health Services Managers

detail.description: Nursing longevity: shift-sleep systems, safe patient-handling technique, debriefing after hard losses, peer support, and choosing units whose pace fits your constitution.
detail.why: Burnout ends more nursing careers than skill does — sustainability habits are clinical skills, not luxuries.
learn: Build a 3-shift sleep rotation system that works for you
Use lift teams and mechanical lifts without exception
Debrief difficult patient outcomes with your team
Keep one non-nursing identity actively alive

detail.description: Nursing licenses are state-issued; the Nurse Licensure Compact (NLC) allows one multistate RN license across member states — renewals, CEUs, and discipline disclosure follow you.
detail.why: Compact status changes where you can work overnight — knowing your state's status matters for travel and relocation plans.
learn: Check whether your state is in the Nurse Licensure Compact
Calendar renewal and CEU requirements
Understand license endorsement when moving states
Keep a clean, disclosable record from day one

detail.description: Nursing is interprofessional: physicians, respiratory therapists, pharmacists, PT/OT, social work, and CNAs — clear role boundaries, closed-loop communication, and mutual respect are the operating system.
detail.why: Patient outcomes track team communication quality; nurses sit at the hub of every shift's coordination.
learn: Practice closed-loop communication on every handoff
Learn each discipline's scope for fast, right referrals
Use structured huddles to start shifts aligned
Debrief conflict professionally, never on the floor

detail.description: The hands-on toolkit: IV insertion and phlebotomy, medication administration (including IV pushes and titration rules), catheters, wounds, and safe medication math.
detail.why: Confidence in core skills is what turns a licensed nurse into a useful one — repetition plus verification builds it.
learn: Practice med math until dose calculations are automatic
Get supervised IV-start reps beyond the minimum
Learn your facility's high-alert medication double-checks
Keep a skills log signed by preceptors
